title: A Night of Empty Nets
lead: Jesus can turn failure into a calling.
questions: In what area of your life do you find it hard, after a failed night, to let down the nets once more on nothing but His word?
Is there someone you are denying their year, pushing them on where Jesus would give them time?
Whom outside the Church could you ask for help, for the use of their boat, before you start preaching anything to them?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Simon had suffered defeat at his own trade, and in front of the whole village: a professional fisherman rinsing empty nets on the shore after a full night’s work. Just then Jesus appears, and He does not start with a sermon but with a request: He borrows Simon’s boat so He can teach from the water. In this way God made a defeated man needed. Then comes an instruction that goes against all of Simon’s experience: “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.” On that lake people fished at night, because by day a school of fish sees both the net and the shadow of the boat. A carpenter is telling a fisherman how to fish. Simon’s answer is one of the most honest sentences about faith in the Bible: “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net” (WEB). He doesn’t fake enthusiasm; he tells the truth about how tired he is, and does what he was asked.

The nets start to tear, a second boat comes to help, and both nearly sink under the load. The miracle happens in the same water where there had been nothing all night; the only thing that had changed was whose word the nets went down on. Simon, however, doesn’t count the fish. He falls to his knees: “Go away from me, Lord,” he says, “for I am a sinful man.” Close to God, people first feel exposed. But Jesus does not go away. He says: “Do not be afraid… From now on you will catch men.” He answers a confession of sin with a calling: where Simon sees a reason to part ways, He sees a qualification for service. The Greek verb here means “to catch alive”: a fish that is caught dies, but a person caught by the gospel is meant to live more fully than before. It is also worth noticing one more thing: “they left everything and followed Him” was not a blind leap by strangers. Simon had known Jesus for about a year by then, by turns walking with Him and going back to the boat. Jesus gave faith time to grow to the size of a decision.

If you are someone who carries a failed night inside, remember that God does not pass over people after a defeat; He chooses them. As a community we need to ask ourselves whether we give seekers the time they need, and to make sure that after our fishing people breathe more fully, not more shallowly.

This part of the series is addressed, among others, to those who have failed. Today we look at the story of a man who suffered defeat in an especially painful way: publicly, and at his own trade. Simon is a professional fisherman on a lake he has known since childhood. He has a boat, partners, gear, and years of experience. He has just come back from a night’s fishing with nothing. He didn’t catch “not much.” He had nothing. Now, in front of the whole village, he is rinsing empty nets, and anyone walking along the shore can see how it went for him. Failing in an unfamiliar field hurts, but failing in your own humiliates. On exactly that day, with the smell of wet, empty nets hanging in the air, Jesus appears.

sections.heading: The Borrowed Boat
paragraphs: Christ starts with a request. The crowd is pressing in on Him right at the water’s edge, so He asks Simon to put out a little way from the shore: the boat will become a pulpit. We do not know the exact location, but it is quite possible that this took place in the bay between Capernaum and Tabgha. The spot looks like a natural amphitheater. A voice carries across the water to people sitting on the slope. And Tabgha is simply a place of seven springs, some of them warm, and in winter the fish gather in these warmer waters, which is why this bit of shoreline was the best fishing ground on the whole lake. The fishermen were exactly where they had the best chance of a good catch, and that night they caught nothing. Before that boat became a pulpit, however, it became something more important: the place where God asked a man for help. Jesus does not begin with a lecture on sin or with a miracle. He begins by making a tired, defeated fisherman needed. He steps into Simon’s world, onto his deck, among his empty nets. It is worth remembering this before we go further: Jesus’ first step toward Simon was not a demand but a request. When God wants to win a person, He begins by respecting who that person is and what they know how to do.

sections.heading: At Your Word
paragraphs: After the sermon comes an instruction that makes no professional sense: “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.” Fishing at night was common practice on the Sea of Galilee. In the dark the nets are invisible to the fish; by day the school sees both the net and the shadow of the boat, and swims off. Besides, the deep-water nets used at night were different gear from the cast nets used by day in the shallows. Simon knows all this better than anyone on the shore. The carpenter from Nazareth is telling a fisherman how to fish, and ordering him to do something his professional experience contradicts: in broad daylight, in deep water, after a night that proved there were no fish. Simon’s answer is one of the most honest statements about faith in the whole Bible: “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net” (WEB). He doesn’t fake enthusiasm. He doesn’t hide that all his experience says otherwise. He tells God the truth about how tired he is, and does what he was asked. Faith is not born where we understand everything. It begins at the point where we don’t understand and let down the nets anyway, because He said so. If everything were obvious, Jesus’ word would not be needed at all.

sections.heading: The Nets Began to Tear
paragraphs: The result exceeds not only expectations but the capacity of the gear. The nets begin to tear, a second boat has to be called over to help, and then both boats, loaded to the gunwales, begin to sink. There is something upside-down in this picture: the only problem of the morning comes from too much blessing. God answered a night of empty nets not by making up the losses, but with an abundance that human logistics could not hold. And notice: the miracle happens in the same water where there had been nothing all night. The lake was still the same. What had changed was whose word the nets were let down on. Same work, same place, same man; the difference lay not in technique but in the Word. That is a lesson for anyone who, after years of work in their “trade,” church work included, has nights of empty nets behind them: abundance does not come from a better method, but from obeying the right voice.

sections.heading: Go Away from Me
paragraphs: Simon’s reaction is surprising. He doesn’t count the fish, doesn’t plan the sale, doesn’t offer Jesus a partnership. He throws himself to his knees among the flapping fish: “Go away from me, Lord,” he says, “for I am a sinful man.” In the abundance he recognized holiness, and it frightened him. Isaiah reacted the same way when he saw the Lord in the temple: “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips.” Close to God, a person does not first feel singled out for honor; they feel seen right through. And here we come to the crux of this story. Jesus does not answer: you’re right, you are sinful, I’ll come back when you’ve improved. He does not go away. He says: “Do not be afraid… From now on you will catch men.” He answers a confession of sin with a calling. Where Simon sees a reason to part ways, Jesus sees a qualification for service. This reversal is good news for anyone who has ever thought that their past, their character, or their failures rule them out of God’s plans. With Jesus, awareness of your own sinfulness does not close the way to a calling. It is its prerequisite: the one who best rescues the drowning is the one who remembers being rescued.

sections.heading: The Year That Is Easy to Forget
paragraphs: “And when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and followed Him.” It sounds like a wild leap into the unknown: a stranger gives the word, and they drop everything. A careful study of the Word, however, shows something else. From John’s account it appears that Simon and his companions had met Jesus about a year earlier, by the Jordan, and since then they had by turns walked with Him and gone back to fishing. The decision over the empty nets was not the reflex of people who did not know Christ. It was the ripe fruit of a year of watching, listening, and testing. Jesus gave them time. He did not demand everything on the first day; He let faith grow to the size of a decision. That is an important correction to the picture we carry in our heads, and a pointer for us when we walk alongside someone on their way to faith: not everyone who still goes back to their nets is undecided. They may simply be halfway through their year. The God who gave Simon twelve months doesn’t need us to hurry anyone along.

There is one more remarkable thing in this calling that the first readers could not have missed. In that world it was the would-be disciple who went looking for a teacher: he came, he asked, he worked to be accepted. The teacher chose the most gifted of them, and the disciple’s goal was to become a teacher himself one day. Jesus turns this whole order upside down. He comes to the water Himself, He does the choosing, and He chooses not from the top students of the schools but from men who work with nets. And He sets a different goal: not “you will be teachers,” but “you will catch men.” He does not offer Simon a career, but the rescue of others.

sections.heading: Caught Alive
paragraphs: In the words “you will catch men” there is one more important detail. The Greek verb Jesus uses literally means “to catch alive.” It was used of taking prisoners who are kept alive, not killed. A fish that is caught dies; a person “caught” by the gospel is meant to live, and to live to the full. The prophets knew the picture of God sending fishermen after people, but as they understood it, it was a picture of coming judgment and exile. Jesus takes the same metaphor and reverses its sign: His fishermen do not lead people to judgment, but pull them out of the deep. That distinction should shape all our thinking about evangelism. If after our “catch” a person is frightened, humiliated, and less alive than before, those were not the right nets. You can recognize fishing for Jesus by this: the one who is caught begins to breathe more fully.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story says three things to anyone who carries a failure, fresh or old. First: Jesus does not pass over people after a failed night; if anything, He chooses them. He did not come to the shore that morning in spite of your failure, but right into the middle of it, because empty nets are where a person is ready to hear more than on a day of success. Second: your defeat is not a verdict. Out of a night that left nothing, Jesus can make the first day of a calling, and out of an embarrassed professional, the most famous fisherman in history. Third: the “do not be afraid” spoken to Simon applies to you as well. Your sinfulness, which you see more sharply the closer you come to Him, does not make Him go away. To us, as a community, this scene puts some of the uncomfortable questions: Do we know how to ask people “on the shore” for help and for their boat before we start instructing them? Do we give seekers time, as Jesus gave it to Simon? Is our fishing a catching alive, after which people live more fully, or just moving fish from one water to another?
